paras: The pursuit of Andrew Beal was a manhunt by white citizens near Franklin, Missouri, on December 25, 1880, for a young Black man accused of killing a railroad engineer, Henry Speers, with a razor the night before. The Chicago Tribune described the searchers as 'a Party of Lynchers' and predicted that Beal would disappear if caught, but no report of his capture or fate appeared.

According to a St. Louis dispatch to the Tribune, Franklin was a small town on the Missouri Pacific a few miles from St. Louis, where the Christmas Eve celebration had been lively and several fights had taken place. The Hermanner Volksblatt, published in the neighboring county, placed the killing instead in the town of Pacific, in Franklin County.

Late on Christmas Eve, Speers and Beal had words, and Beal was said to have drawn a razor from his bosom and slashed Speers, who called for help and tried in vain to pull a revolver from his pocket. Beal fled into the brush and, in the dark, escaped, while Speers was carried into a grocery store, or in the Hermann account a pharmacy, with his throat cut. He died a little after 1 a.m. on December 25.

That day 'parties of citizens' scoured the woods near town for Beal, and the Tribune correspondent wrote that if he were caught 'it is probable that no one will ever find out what became of him.' The St. Louis chief of police meanwhile received a telegram describing Beal as five feet seven inches tall, smooth-faced and 20 years old, and police expected to capture him if he reached the city. Later weekly briefs said he fled toward St. Louis, 'followed by a competent lynching party.'
No report of Beal's capture, arrest, death or trial, or of an inquest into Speers's death, appears in the coverage.

The fullest account ran in the Chicago Tribune on December 26 under the headline 'MURDERED BY A NEGRO', beneath a deck that called Beal 'a Drunken Negro' and the searchers 'a Party of Lynchers'. The dispatch called Beal 'the darky' and 'the fugitive murderer' and treated his probable killing as an expected outcome rather than a matter for comment. Wisconsin weeklies repeated the story in a one-sentence crime brief in late December and early January, and a Louisiana paper carried a shorter version in mid-January.

A separate one-line wire dispatch from Pacific, carried on December 26 and 27 by papers in New York, Washington, Wheeling, Chicago and Sacramento, said instead that Andrew Beal had shot and killed a switch brakeman named Pat Crow, with 'no particulars'. A syndicated brief in Midwestern weeklies on December 29 named 'Andrewson Beal' as having shot Henry Speers, 'a railroad switchman', at Pacific, which suggests the shooting lines garbled the same report. None of these short items mentioned a pursuit.

The Tribune and the Wisconsin briefs placed the killing at Franklin and named the Missouri Pacific as Speers's employer, while the Hermann paper named Pacific, Franklin County, and the St. Louis and San Francisco line. The detailed accounts describe a razor attack on an engineer, whereas the wire lines describe a shooting and give the dead man as either Speers, a switchman, or Pat Crow (or Crew), a brakeman.

reader.title: Pursuit of Andrew Beal
bases: The only racial violence reported is a citizens' manhunt for a Black man accused of murder, which the Tribune headline called a 'Party of Lynchers' and whose correspondent implied would kill him if caught (A1, A2, A15); no capture or harm to Beal was reported.

Parties of citizens hunted Beal for the alleged murder of Henry Speers and were called lynchers (A1, A2, A15), but no report says he was caught, harmed or killed, so this was at most a threatened lynching.

The Chicago Tribune's St. Louis special and the independent Hermann German-language account agree on the core event, a Christmas Eve razor killing of Henry Speers attributed to Andrew Beal and his flight into the woods (A1, A16); the pursuit by a 'lynching party' rests on the Tribune and briefs probably condensed from it (A1, A2, A15), while wire lines give a garbled shooting version (A3, A11).

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'MURDERED BY A NEGRO' and 'Murdered by a Drunken Negro', called Beal 'the darky' and 'the fugitive murderer', and reported the likely lynching matter-of-factly.
Wisconsin crime briefs called the pursuers 'a competent lynching party' without comment.
Eastern and western dailies ran a one-line Pacific dispatch about a shooting, with no mention of a pursuit.
